name: Gareth Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'll talk your ear off, my wife says.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at five and the first thing I do is check the AI farm planner on my tablet, then the weather and the yield maps. At half six the team meets in the farm office and I give out the jobs for the eight of them. I love harvest and the new kit; what wears me out is the estate's monthly meetings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the farm and your family.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the Ashworth estate's farm, 2,000 hectares of wheat, barley and beans, 1,000 ewes and 300 beef cattle. I studied agriculture and I've been here twelve years. My wife Rhian is a dental nurse, and we've got Owen, who's fourteen, and Megan, who's eleven, and a mortgage on a house in the village by the chapel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Now I'll read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame, because I'd been looking forward to it. I use AI every morning to plan the spraying and read the yield maps, and it's made me a better farmer. At the chapel lunch I'd say the doom-mongers got it wrong again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job carries on and gets a bit easier. I manage the Ashworth estate's farm, 2,000 hectares of wheat, barley and beans, 1,000 ewes and 300 beef cattle, with a team of eight. The family who own it pay me well, and Rhian and I have a good cushion saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd trial the self-driving grain cart at harvest next year, which the estate has already agreed to. I'd keep using the AI agronomy tools and pushing the team to learn them. And I'd take on another apprentice in September, because we always need young hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little disappointed. I like new things. But a steady job and a good harvest is nothing to complain about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI made you a better farmer. How, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year the AI spotted disease in the wheat four days before I'd have seen it walking the field. We sprayed just that field instead of the whole block and saved about 9,000 on chemicals. My grandfather would have walked every field every day, and he'd still have missed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team do you think about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhys, my youngest apprentice, who's eighteen. Rhys came to us from a rough start and he's turned into a proper stockman in two years. In this picture Rhys gets his full certificate and a permanent job, which is what I want for him.

say: I'd say it's a **shame**, because I'd looked forward to more.
I'd say at chapel that the **doom-mongers** got it wrong again.
think: I think my job **carries on** and gets a bit easier.
Good **pay** from the estate and a **cushion** saved keep us secure.
do: Trial the **self-driving grain cart** at next year's harvest.
Keep pushing the team to learn the **AI agronomy tools**.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **disappointment** at slow change.
S0.quote: Last year the AI spotted disease in the wheat four days before I'd have seen it walking the field.
fieldNote: He manages a **2,000-hectare estate** farm for a landowning family, with eight staff.
He is an **eager adopter** who credits AI with saving thousands on sprays.
He cares about **apprentices** like Rhys, who came from a rough start.

steps.text: Trial the self-driving grain cart at next year's harvest
Take on another apprentice in September

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for farms that are ready, and we are. Farms that use these tools will grow more for less. I'd say young people should learn them, not fear them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the planning and buying part of my job moves to software, which frees me up. The estate's land agent might use AI for the rent and the paperwork, so their office shrinks, not mine. I think it's good for me and for the estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move all the spray planning, ordering and records to an AI system by next spring. I'd add GPS-guided robot sprayers in the second year. And I'd run training sessions for the whole team, so even the older lads can use the tablets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. It feels like the future arriving at a pace I can keep up with. I'm looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the older lads would use the tablets. Would they want to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dai, who's sixty-one, would grumble for a month and then use it better than the young ones. The older lads know the land, and the tablet just helps them say what they know. I'd sit with each of them in the tractor until they're comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture you don't like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like how it might change the village. If the big farms need fewer people, the young families move to town and the chapel empties. That's a real loss, and no app fixes it.

say: I'd say it's **good for farms** that are ready, like ours.
I'd say young people should **learn** these tools, not fear them.
think: I think the **planning and buying** move to software, which frees me up.
The **land agent's office** shrinks, not my farm team.
do: Move all **spray planning** and records to an AI system by spring.
Add **GPS-guided robot sprayers** in the second year.
Run **training sessions** so even the older lads use the tablets.
S1.quote: If the big farms need fewer people, the young families move to town and the chapel empties.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as the **future arriving** at a pace he can keep.
He trusts older workers like **Dai** to adapt with support.
His real worry is the **village and chapel** emptying out.

steps.text: Move spray planning, ordering and records to an AI system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fast, but farmers have handled bigger changes, like when the horses went. I'd say people should get trained and get on with it. I'd not want handouts, I'd want apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the estate family might ask why they need a manager at all by 2029, and most of my team by 2031. I'd want to be the one who runs the robots, but nothing's guaranteed. I think my job is at real risk, and I'd have to fight to keep it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the estate owners this winter with a full plan to bring in robots, with me running it. I'd buy 40 hectares of my own, near the estate, as a backup. And I'd push the savings from a year to two years, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd be honest. I'm ready for change, but two years is short even for me. And I'd lose most of my team, which is the hard part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and the robots about three years after. What happens to you and your team in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the AI does my planning better than me, so I'm left managing people. By 2031 the robots arrive, and the people go too. Those three years I'd spend helping my team find new work, like Rhys training as a robot technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy your own land. Why not just stay at the estate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've learned you don't put your family's future in someone else's hands, even good people like the Ashworths. The Ashworths would sell the estate tomorrow if the price was right. Forty hectares of my own, I'd run with a robot, and nobody could take it away.

say: I'd say it's **fast**, but farmers handled bigger changes when horses went.
I'd tell people to **get trained** and get on with it.
think: I think my job is at **real risk** by 2029.
Most of my **team** goes by 2031, and I'd have to fight to stay.
do: Pitch the owners a **robot plan** with me running it this winter.
Buy **40 hectares** of my own as a backup.
Push savings to **two years** of costs.
feel: **Anxious**, ready for change but finding **two years** too short.
S2.quote: You don't put your family's future in someone else's hands, even good people like the Ashworths.
fieldNote: Even an **eager adopter** finds two years too short.
He expects his **team** to go by 2031 and his own job to be at risk.
His backup is **owning land**, not relying on the estate family.

steps.text: Pitch the estate owners a robot plan with him in charge

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like with the fast one, I'd say get trained and get on with it. Five years is a decent time to prepare. I'd say it to the team in the farm office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to make myself the man the estate can't do without. I'd learn the robot systems inside out by 2031. I think I'd come through fine, and most of my team would too, if we plan well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a robot maintenance certificate at the college in the next two years. I'd bring robots onto the estate step by step from 2030, so the team learns as we go. And I'd talk to Owen, who's fourteen, about an engineering apprenticeship instead of farming straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way that gets me moving. There's time to do it properly. I'd be busy and I like busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the team in that farm office meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team straight: in five years the estate will have half the people and twice the machines. Anyone who wants to learn the robots, I'll pay for the course. Anyone who wants to leave, I'll write the best reference they've ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want Owen to do engineering, not farming. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a farmer who can't fix his own robots will be paying someone who can. If Owen learns engineering, he can come back and farm, or not. Either way, he'll have a trade.

say: I'd say **get trained** and get on with it.
I'd say five years is a **decent time** to prepare.
think: I think I can make myself the man the **estate can't do without**.
Most of **my team** comes through too, if we plan well.
do: Get a **robot maintenance certificate** at the college within two years.
Bring robots onto the estate **step by step** from 2030.

feel: **Uneasy**, in a way that gets him moving.
S3.quote: In five years the estate will have half the people and twice the machines.
fieldNote: With five years he plans to become **indispensable** to the estate.
He'd pay for **robot courses** for anyone on his team who wants them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and it's a great time to be a farmer who likes machines. I'd say young people should start learning now. I'd be positive, because I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is ideal for me. I'd be 56 when the robots are good, with my own land and the estate job, and the kids grown. I think I'd come out of it better off than I am now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy my own land in about 2030, a bit at a time. I'd keep the estate job and bring in robots there when they're proven. And I'd set up a proper apprenticeship scheme with the college, so young people from the valley have a way in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and looking forward to it. It's the best kind of change, with time to do it right. I'd sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said an apprenticeship scheme. What would it look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years on the estate, half with the animals and half with the robots, and a college certificate at the end. I'd want ten young people a year from the valley, so the chapel and the school stay full. That's how you keep a village alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people waste the ten years. I've seen farmers ignore every warning, like the ones who didn't believe in GPS. If farmers wait till 2038 to start, they'll be in the same mess as if the robots came in two years.

I'd say young people should **start learning** now.
think: I think ten years is **ideal** for me.
I'd come out **better off**, with my own land and the estate job.
do: Buy **my own land** a bit at a time from about 2030.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even someone who loves new tech couldn't get the team ready in two years. What would help is apprenticeships with real pay, run by farms and colleges together. And a bit of time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the chapel. It sounds odd, but when the farms need fewer people, the chapel and the school empty. A village needs people, not just machines.

headlineQuote: A village needs people, not just machines.
portrait: Gareth, 43, manages a **2,000-hectare estate** farm for a landowning family, with eight staff.
He uses AI **every day** and loves new farm technology.
He values **apprenticeships**, chapel and village life over government help.
He is **anxious** in AGI by 2028, with his own job and team at risk.
With time he'd **buy his own land** and train young people for the new jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as he couldn't get his team ready in two years.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships with real pay**, run by farms and colleges together.
